title: Development depends on the constraints between people and markets
dek: A new childcare-delivery experiment, a peer-reviewed infrastructure study, and a classic experiment on the informal tax imposed by kin.
trend: Across Uganda, Burkina Faso, and Kenya, the binding constraint is rarely just a missing asset. Childcare can free market vendors' time, but location determines take-up and whether gains appear in earnings or family well-being. Electricity reaches relatively few homes, yet changes water systems, schools, communications, and finance for whole communities. Informal kin obligations can operate like a tax on visible income, causing women to conceal resources and forgo returns. The broader trend is access plus social structure: public investments work through delivery choices, spillovers, and household relationships that determine who can use a service and how much of its return they can keep.

articles.summary: A randomized comparison of workplace- and community-based childcare for 883 women market vendors in Kampala finds gains in hourly earnings, well-being, and child development, with different delivery models reaching different women and producing different mixes of benefits.

paper.title: Childcare for Informal-Sector Workers: Delivery Models, Access, and Welfare
paper.authors: Jacklyn Makaaru Arinaitwe; George Bogere; Anna Fiore; Sylvan Herskowitz; Megan Lang; Francis Mwesigye; Tracy Nalumansi
paper.source: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11442
paper.abstract: A randomized comparison of free workplace- and community-based childcare for 883 women market vendors in Kampala finds higher hourly earnings, well-being, and child development, with meaningful delivery-model trade-offs.

articles.summary: Engineering-driven differences in the timing of Burkina Faso's grid rollout show that electrification can improve local public goods, communications, and financial inclusion even when most households do not connect.

paper.title: Community Effects of Electrification: Evidence from Burkina Faso's Grid Extension
paper.abstract: Burkina Faso's engineering-driven grid rollout increased nighttime light, school electrification, water infrastructure, appliance ownership, and financial inclusion, including spillovers to unconnected households.

articles.summary: A lab-in-the-field experiment in rural Kenya reveals that women sacrifice expected investment returns to conceal income from relatives, quantifying social pressure to share as an informal tax on visible resources.

paper.title: Does Africa Need a Rotten Kin Theorem? Experimental Evidence from Village Economies
paper.abstract: A lab-in-the-field experiment in rural Kenya finds that women sacrifice expected investment returns to hide income from relatives and neighbors, implying a measurable informal tax on visible resources.

title: Policies change the system around them
dek: Two peer-reviewed development papers on environmental substitution and post-conflict reconstruction, plus a classic health-accountability experiment.
trend: These papers treat policy as a change to an interacting system. China's straw-burning ban cleans the air but induces farmers to use more chemicals, shifting damage into water. Afghan demining removes a physical barrier and produces reinforcing gains in land use, local activity, and security. Uganda's community-monitoring experiment changes the information and accountability facing health workers, improving effort and child outcomes without adding major resources. The broader trend is to trace behavioral responses, spillovers, and complementary institutions: net effects depend on what people substitute toward and whether surrounding systems amplify or dilute the intervention.

articles.summary: China's staggered straw-burning ban reduced fires and air pollution, but induced fertilizer and pesticide substitution that worsened water pollution and offset much of the estimated health benefit.

paper.title: When the Fire Ends: Straw Burning, Regulation, and Pollution Substitution
paper.abstract: Using China's staggered prohibition on crop-residue burning, the paper shows that lower agricultural fires and air pollution were partly offset by greater fertilizer and pesticide use and worse water pollution.

articles.summary: Geocoded clearance records and modern staggered event studies show that Afghan demining increased nighttime lights and productive land use while lowering nearby conflict risk.

paper.title: Landmine Clearance and Economic Development: Evidence from Multispectral Satellite Imagery, Nighttime Lights, and Conflict Events in Afghanistan
paper.authors: Ariel BenYishay; Rachel Sayers; Kunwar Singh; Christian Baehr; Madeleine Walker
paper.abstract: Geocoded clearance records for more than 15,000 Afghan hazardous areas show that demining increased nighttime lights and productive land use while reducing nearby conflict risk.

articles.summary: Randomized report cards and facilitated meetings increased citizen monitoring of Ugandan clinics, improved provider effort and utilization, and raised child health and survival.

paper.title: Power to the People: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment on Community-Based Monitoring in Uganda
paper.abstract: A randomized community-monitoring intervention in Uganda improved health-worker effort, clinic use, infant weight, and under-five survival.

title: Interventions meet the constraints beneath them
dek: A peer-reviewed Uganda procurement study, a randomized digital-outreach experiment with Venezuelan migrants in Colombia, and a classic Sri Lankan capital experiment.
trend: Across all three papers, policies work only when they meet the binding constraint. Public contracts in Uganda raise sales but crowd out private customers without improving productivity; WhatsApp information in Colombia lowers migrants' program take-up because content and unsolicited contact create friction; and the Sri Lankan classic shows that capital grants generate high returns where credit is genuinely scarce. The shared lesson is to identify the constraint an intervention relaxes—and the new friction it may create—rather than treating more demand, information, or money as interchangeable.

articles.summary: Ugandan administrative records and a staggered event study show that government contracts raise total sales but displace private-market sales and do not improve value added per worker. A firm survey points to capacity limits, higher public prices, and delayed payments.

paper.title: Government Demand and Firm Growth
paper.authors: Bernard Hoekman; Marco Sanfilippo; Filippo Santi; Rohit Ticku
paper.abstract: Ugandan tax and procurement records show that firms' sales rise after they first sell to government, but private-market sales fall and value added per worker does not improve. A staggered event study and a mechanism survey point to capacity constraints, higher public-sector prices, and payment delays.

articles.summary: In a randomized WhatsApp experiment, informational videos reduced Venezuelan migrants' take-up of Colombia's regularization program by 8 percentage points. Procedural content discouraged viewers, while unsolicited contact discouraged some non-viewers.

paper.title: When Digital Nudges Nag: Evidence on Program Take-up from a WhatsApp Intervention
paper.authors: Maria José Urbina; Andrés Moya; Sandra V. Rozo
paper.source: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11423
paper.abstract: A randomized WhatsApp intervention for undocumented Venezuelan migrants in Colombia reduced take-up of a regularization program by 8 percentage points. Procedural information discouraged viewers and unsolicited contact discouraged non-viewers, especially among people initially near the enrollment margin.

articles.summary: Random cash and equipment grants to Sri Lankan microenterprises reveal monthly real returns near 5 percent, with larger returns for owners facing tighter credit constraints. The evidence favors missing credit over missing insurance as the central bottleneck.

paper.title: Returns to Capital in Microenterprises: Evidence from a Field Experiment
paper.authors: Suresh de Mel; David McKenzie; Christopher Woodruff
paper.abstract: Random cash and equipment grants to low-capital Sri Lankan microenterprises identify monthly real returns of roughly 5 percent, with larger returns among owners facing tighter credit constraints. The experiment tests spillovers, reporting changes, grant form, nonlinearities, and heterogeneous returns.

title: When climate and institutions narrow the feasible set
dek: Two peer-reviewed development-economics studies on climate and malaria, plus a classic natural experiment on business registration in Mexico.
trend: Across all three papers, shocks and rules matter because they change the set of choices people can actually afford. In rural India, warming reduces agricultural resources and appears to constrict marriage-related migration, particularly where dowry norms are strongest. In Rwanda, weather-suited malaria exposure depresses high-stakes test performance and widens a gender gap, while bed nets soften the loss. Bruhn's Mexican classic supplies the institutional counterpoint: cutting registration costs creates firms and jobs, but mainly by inducing wage earners to become entrepreneurs rather than by formalizing incumbents.

articles.summary: A district panel combining three Indian censuses, household surveys, and local weather links long-run warming to less marriage-related female migration, especially in high-dowry areas. Lower crop yields, consumption, and dowry resources are plausible channels; the principal caveat is that the design relies on observational district-panel variation.

paper.title: Scorching Heat and Shrinking Horizons: The Impact of Rising Temperatures on Marriages and Migration in Rural India
paper.authors: Manisha Mukherjee; Bruno Martorano; Melissa Siegel
paper.abstract: A district panel combining Indian census, household survey, and local weather data finds that rising long-run temperatures reduce women's rural-rural and rural-urban migration, especially in high-dowry areas. Lower agricultural yields, consumption, and dowry resources are plausible mechanisms.

articles.summary: More than one million Rwandan exam records are matched to weather-driven malaria suitability. Exposure predicts substantially lower test performance and a wider gender gap, while bed-net coverage attenuates the losses; extensive timing, placebo, migration, and spatial-error checks support the result.

paper.title: Malaria and Human Capital Accumulation
paper.authors: Abenezer Z. Aklilu; Justice Tei Mensah; Aimable Nsabimana
paper.abstract: More than one million Rwandan primary-school exam records are matched to weather-driven malaria suitability. Exposure predicts lower scores, with larger losses for girls; insecticide-treated bed nets attenuate the damage. The paper reports extensive weather, disease-placebo, migration, and spatial-error checks.

articles.summary: Staggered adoption of Mexico's one-stop registration system increased registered businesses by about 5 percent and employment in eligible industries by about 2.8 percent. The new firms came mainly from former wage earners, not from incumbent informal owners, while greater competition lowered prices and incumbents' income.

paper.title: License to Sell: The Effect of Business Registration Reform on Entrepreneurial Activity in Mexico
paper.source: The Review of Economics and Statistics 93(1)
paper.abstract: Staggered adoption of Mexico's rapid-business-opening system increased registered businesses by about 5 percent and employment in eligible industries by about 2.8 percent. New firms came mainly from former wage earners rather than incumbent informal owners, while competition lowered prices and incumbent income.

title: What access unlocks - and what it does not
dek: Two randomized development-economics studies on education and factory work, plus a classic disaster-economics paper on opportunity costs and institutions.
trend: This issue asks when access is genuinely productive. In rural India, access to either better classroom instruction or community study groups is insufficient by itself; the two inputs become effective when combined. In Ethiopia, removing application frictions opens factory employment and raises welfare briefly, but does not create a durable earnings ladder. Kenny's classic shows the same discipline at a systems level: safer construction matters, yet scarce budgets and weak enforcement make targeting and institutions as important as engineering.

articles.summary: A cross-cutting cluster-randomized experiment across 200 villages in Assam finds that in-school targeted pedagogy and community-managed study groups raise learning only when combined. The full program increases math scores by 0.11 standard deviations and language by 0.09 at modest cost; mechanisms and external validity are the main caveats.

paper.title: Supporting Learning In and Out of School: Experimental Evidence from India
paper.abstract: A cross-cutting cluster-randomized experiment across 200 villages in Assam finds that in-school targeted pedagogy and community-managed study groups produce learning gains only when combined. The full program raises math scores by 0.11 standard deviations and language by 0.09 at modest cost.

articles.summary: Randomized application support for 687 young women seeking work in an Ethiopian industrial park raises short-run employment, earnings, and savings. Four years later the control group has caught up and early health costs have faded, suggesting that entry frictions were real but the jobs were not durable ladders out of poverty.

paper.title: Do Factory Jobs Improve Welfare? Experimental Evidence from Ethiopia
paper.authors: Girum Abebe; Niklas Buehren; Markus Goldstein
paper.abstract: Randomized job-application support for 687 young women in Ethiopia raises short-run employment, earnings, and savings, but the advantages dissipate by the four-year follow-up as control applicants find alternatives. Early health costs also fade.

articles.summary: Charles Kenny uses benefit-cost reasoning and political economy to explain why preventable earthquake deaths remain concentrated in poorer countries. The paper favors targeted retrofits, simple enforceable codes, and oversight of public construction; it is a policy synthesis rather than a modern causal design, but its opportunity-cost framing remains highly useful.

paper.title: Why Do People Die in Earthquakes? The Costs Benefits and Institutions of Disaster Risk Reduction in Developing Countries
paper.source: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 4823
paper.abstract: A classic disaster-development paper uses benefit-cost reasoning and political economy to explain why preventable earthquake deaths remain concentrated in poorer countries and argues for targeted retrofits, enforceable codes, and oversight of public construction.

title: Warnings, clean care, and emergency access
dek: Two development-focused reads on the last mile of disaster protection and safe health care, plus an EMS access comparison.
trend: This issue's common thread is that nominal coverage is not operational access. Disaster warnings save lives only when poorer and less-connected households receive and can act on them. Clinics cannot deliver safe care without water, sanitation, waste management, and cleaning - basic inputs whose absence creates a large hidden health and economic burden across African countries. Rural ambulance systems show the same last-mile problem in a richer setting: formal coverage can coexist with response times nearly twice as long.

articles.summary: Combining the World Risk Poll's roughly 147,000 respondents in 142 countries with household surveys and Indonesian village data, the authors ask who receives disaster warnings and what happens afterward. Coverage rises with national income, while education, dwelling location, and digital access shape reception within countries. Warning receipt is associated with more preventive action and higher perceived resilience; villages with warning systems have casualty rates estimated at roughly one-fifth those without them. The evidence is strongly policy-relevant but largely observational.

paper.title: Early Warnings Coverage, Determinants of Reception, and Benefits: What Surveys Can Tell Us
paper.authors: Chloe Beaudet; Louise Bernard; Bramka Arga Jafino; Paolo Avner
paper.source: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11199
paper.abstract: Using four surveys at international, national, and subnational scales, this paper examines who receives early disaster warnings and the benefits associated with reception. Coverage rises with GDP per capita and varies within countries by socioeconomic status, location, education, and digital access. Warning reception is associated with greater perceived resilience, more preventive action, and lower casualty rates in disaster-affected areas.

articles.summary: A cost-of-illness model for nine Eastern and Southern African countries estimates 3.1 million health care-associated infections and more than 320,000 excess deaths in 2022. The modeled economic burden exceeds $6 billion, or 1.14 percent of combined GDP, while basic water, sanitation, hygiene, waste management, and cleaning investments yield an estimated benefit-cost ratio of 5.8. The estimates necessarily rely on sparse surveillance data and cross-country extrapolation.

paper.title: Costs of Health Care Associated Infections from Inadequate Water and Sanitation in Health Care Facilities in Eastern and Southern Africa
paper.authors: Guy Hutton; Claire Chase; Ruth Kennedy Walker
paper.source: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 10708
paper.abstract: A cost-of-illness model for nine Eastern and Southern African countries estimates 3.1 million health care-associated infections and more than 320000 excess deaths in 2022. The modeled economic burden exceeds US$6 billion or 1.14 percent of combined GDP, while comprehensive WASH, waste management, and cleaning investments have an estimated benefit-cost ratio of 5.8.

articles.summary: Town-level Connecticut data show rural mean EMS response time near 13 minutes - roughly twice the non-rural mean - while median household income does not explain variation within either group. Geography, stationing, staffing, and volunteer-service capacity look more plausible than town income alone. The evidence is descriptive rather than causal and uses 2016 data.

paper.title: Socioeconomic factors influencing rural-urban ambulance response time disparities in Connecticut
paper.abstract: Abstract Across the U.S, it is a documented fact that rural areas have longer ambulance response times and tend to have lower median income. The objective of this study was to test if the rural-urban emergency medical service (EMS) response time disparity was related to wealth disparity in the state of Connecticut. All mean EMS response times were sourced from the 2016 Office of Emergency Medical Services Data Report. Rural definitions were sourced from the Connecticut Office of Rural Health. Median income data was drawn from the Connecticut Office of Policy and Management. A Mann-Whitney U test determined if the average rural EMS response time was greater than the non-rural EMS response time. Pearson coefficients quantified the relationship between median income and EMS response time. A t-test ascertained if the average median income differed between the two datasets. The mean EMS response time was 12.98 min (SD = 3.36) rural and 8.26 min (SD = 2.12) non-rural. Rural mean response time and median income were not significantly correlated ( r = -.148, p =.247); non-rural mean response time and median income were also not significantly related. No significant disparity was detected (t=0.478, p =.633) between the mean rural household income ($98,258) and mean non-rural household income ($95,706). Significant disparities in EMS response times can exist between rural and non-rural towns separate from median income trends, as is the case in Connecticut. These findings may have limited generalizability because of Connecticut’s relatively high median income as compared to other states yet may be relevant to states with similar economic metrics.
